Exam focus (doctor): terminology and core concepts from the slides, more than cancer-specific staging detail.

Objectives

  • Define common terminology related to neoplasia and malignant transformation.
  • Differentiate benign from malignant tumors; describe the major mechanisms of local invasion and metastatic spread.
  • Explain the basic principles of cancer diagnosis, grading, and TNM staging.
  • Describe the roles of surgery in cancer: curative, diagnostic, prophylactic, cytoreductive, palliative.
  • Differentiate neoadjuvant, adjuvant, systemic, radiation, and local/regional therapies within multidisciplinary care.

1. Basic terminology

  • Neoplasia: new tissue growth that is unregulated, irreversible, and monoclonal — these features distinguish it from hyperplasia and repair.
  • Hyperplasia: increased number of cells.
  • Hypertrophy: increased cell size.
  • Metaplasia: replacement of one differentiated cell type by another.
  • Dysplasia: abnormal cellular growth and maturation.
  • Neoplasia: autonomous abnormal proliferation.
ProcessDoctor's key point
Hypertrophy↑ cell size, no change in number — e.g. cardiac hypertrophy in chronic hypertension
Hyperplasia↑ cell number by a regulated stimulus (estrogen/androgen) — regulated and reversible once the stimulus is removed, unlike neoplasia
NeoplasiaUnregulated, irreversible; usually monoclonal — one mutated cell accumulates more mutations over years
Metaplasiae.g. Barrett esophagus: squamous → columnar (chronic acid reflux)
DysplasiaDisordered proliferation with atypia (pleomorphism); end result of persistent metaplasia; premalignant if the stimulus persists

Neoplasia progression

  • Normal → Metaplasia → Dysplasia → Carcinoma in situ → Invasive carcinoma → Metastasis
  • Neoplasm ≠ cancer — a neoplasm may be benign or malignant (e.g. lipoma = benign neoplasm with essentially no invasion/metastasis).
  • Carcinoma in situ = full-thickness dysplasia that stays above the basement membrane; invasive carcinoma = malignant cells breach the basement membrane.
  • Progression does not always follow a fixed normal → hyperplasia → metaplasia → dysplasia → cancer sequence.
  • Premalignant polyp = adenomatous (not hamartomatous, inflammatory or hyperplastic). 427

2. Benign vs malignant

FeatureBenignMalignant
DifferentiationUsually well differentiatedVariable / poorly differentiated
GrowthUsually slowOften faster
Local invasionNoYes
MetastasisNoPossible
RecurrenceUsually uncommonMay occur
Clinical impactUsually localLocal + systemic
  • Well differentiated: closely resembles the tissue of origin, better prognosis. Poorly differentiated: minimal resemblance; special stains may be needed.
  • Undifferentiated / anaplastic tumors carry the worst prognosis.

3. Carcinogenesis

FactorExamplesAssociated malignancy
Inherited geneticBRCA1/BRCA2 mutations; APC mutation (FAP)Breast/ovarian cancer; colorectal cancer
DietHigh intake of processed/red meat; smoked and preserved foodsColorectal cancer; gastric cancer
Residential environmentRadon exposure in homesLung cancer
Work environmentAsbestos; aromatic amines in dye/rubber industriesMesothelioma/lung cancer; bladder cancer
LifestyleSmoking; alcoholLung and many other cancers; liver, upper GI
Ionising radiationPrevious radiotherapy; high environmental radiationLeukemia, thyroid cancer, various solid tumors
CarcinogensAflatoxin B1; benzeneHepatocellular carcinoma; leukemia
Viral infectionHPV; HBV/HCVCervical/anal/oropharyngeal; hepatocellular carcinoma
HormonalProlonged estrogen; androgen signallingEndometrial/breast; prostate
Increasing ageAccumulation of somatic mutationsMost cancers (colorectal, prostate, pancreatic)
  • Cancer usually results from multiple accumulated genetic errors.
  • APC mutation = earliest event in the adenoma–carcinoma sequence.
  • Radiation → secondary malignancy often ~20 years later (e.g. angiosarcoma in a previously irradiated field).
  • Trend: occupational cancers are less common now; late treatment-related cancers are seen more because survival has improved.
  • BRCA1 → breast cancer. 437 ×3 436
  • H. pylori carries the risk of upper GI contamination and neoplasia (commonest cause of peptic ulcer and gastric adenocarcinoma). 431 ×3
  • Ulcerative colitis definitely increases colon cancer risk (more than Crohn's in this old question). 427
  • HCC risk factors: cirrhosis, hepatitis B (and C); smoking was keyed as the "except" (least risk) — note hepatitis A does not cause HCC. 426
  • HCC paraneoplastic syndromes: hypoglycemia, hypercalcemia, hypercholesterolemia, erythrocytosis — not hyperglycemia. 426

4. Genetic mutations

  • Germline: inherited/heritable predisposition present throughout the body.
  • Somatic: acquired mutation arising in particular cells during life.
  • Germline mutation can arise de novo, with no previous family history.
SomaticGermline
LocationOnly in tumor cellsThroughout the body's normal cells
Inherited?Not necessarilyYes — hereditary predisposition
TestingTumor tissue (guides targeted therapy)Blood or normal tissue
ImplicationTreatment selection↑ risk of multiple different cancers
  • FAP: APC mutation + family history → germline testing; predisposes to colorectal and other tumors (small bowel, thyroid).
  • Lynch syndrome: microsatellite instability (MSI)/MMR deficiency; colorectal + extracolonic cancers (ovarian, pancreatic). Germline. Family history may be absent — a young patient with colorectal cancer should raise suspicion. New CRCs get routine MSI/MMR testing → abnormal → germline testing.
  • DNA mismatch repair: MMR proteins repair daily replication errors; deficiency → mutations accumulate → genomic instability → cancer.
  • Clues for hereditary cancer: young age, family history, characteristic tumor pattern, syndrome criteria.

5. Surgical oncology — the field

  • Field of surgery concerned with the diagnosis, staging, and surgical management of cancer, integrating surgery with other oncologic therapies.
  • Risk assessment → Diagnosis → Staging → Treatment planning → Surgery → Adjuvant therapy decisions → Surveillance/Survivorship.
  • Far more than operating: diagnosis, risk assessment, staging, surgery, MDT/tumor board, integration with medical/radiation oncology, prevention, surveillance.

6. Prevention

Prophylactic surgery

  • Surgery may be done before cancer develops in patients with a sufficiently high risk:
    • FAP → prophylactic colectomy/proctocolectomy.
    • BRCA1/BRCA2 → risk-reducing bilateral mastectomy and/or salpingo-oophorectomy.
  • FAP: prophylactic total colectomy may be needed in young patients with extensive polyposis. BRCA1 carriers have a very high lifetime risk; risk-reducing surgery markedly reduces it in counselled patients. Prevention may also be medical/hormonal.

Screening

  • Breast → mammography. Cervical → HPV testing ± Pap smear. Colorectal → FIT, colonoscopy. Prostate → PSA.
  • A screening test should be sensitive, specific, acceptable, detect cancer at a stage when early treatment is beneficial, and be cost-effective.
  • Colonoscopy is the best colorectal screening tool — sensitive/specific and allows polypectomy; its limitation as a national program is cost.
  • Average-risk colorectal screening (no family history) → colonoscopy every 10 years starting at 45–50. 441 Final
  • Lung cancer screening → annual low-dose CT for age 50–80 with ≥ 20 pack-years who smoke now or quit within 15 years: e.g. a 52-year-old, 30 pack-years, quit 10 years ago 442 Final; the only candidate among the choices was the 51-year-old with 30 pack-years (others too young or too few pack-years). 441 Final
  • Stool testing (average risk): occult blood → positive → colonoscopy; repeated periodically.
  • High-risk rule: first-degree relative with CRC at 40 → start colonoscopy at ~30 (10 years earlier than the relative).
  • Screening = detect cancer in its early stages, when treatment is possible. 439

7. Diagnosis

  • History and physical examination: crucial for risk assessment and guiding therapy — symptoms/signs of the primary tumor (local), systemic consequences, metastatic disease; risk factors and family history; functional status; tumor markers.
  • History: alarm symptoms (weight loss, fever, appetite loss), family history, smoking/alcohol, previous radiation, local symptoms (GI bleeding, dysphagia, breast), regional/distant (ascites, jaundice).
  • Examination: general appearance + performance status (every patient), breast palpation, PR/DRE for rectal cancer, abdomen for ascites/masses, fitness for surgery/chemo, curative vs palliative intent.
  • 70-year-old with bright red blood mixed with stool, weight loss, constipation, pallor → colon cancer (adenocarcinoma). 436 ×5 430
  • 62-year-old with hematochezia and 3rd-degree hemorrhoids → colonoscopy first (rule out cancer before treating the hemorrhoids). 435

  • Exam trap: tumor markers have different purposes — they are not interchangeable and not universally diagnostic.
  • CEA = tumor marker of colorectal cancer, most useful for surveillance of recurrence (not screening). 436 441 437 ×2 436
  • Pancreatic head tumor → CA 19-9. 436
  • Prostate → PSA (also the marker for follow-up after prostate-cancer treatment). 436 439 Final
  • Palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier) → tumor of the head of the pancreas, not a CBD stone. 427

Imaging & endoscopy

  • Diagnostic imaging: US, mammogram, CT, MRI. Endoscopic assessment: upper endoscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy.
  • Sequence rule: do not stage before confirming the diagnosis: suspicious lesion → imaging → biopsy → confirm malignancy → staging.
BI-RADSMeaning
0Incomplete → additional imaging
1Negative
2Benign
3Probably benign → short-interval follow-up
4Suspicious
5Highly suggestive of malignancy
6Biopsy-proven malignancy
  • Suspected brain tumor: initial investigation CT (old key; MRI is the definitive study). 427
  • Thyroid nodule on exam/US → next step FNA. 427
  • Firm fixed posterior-triangle neck swelling in an old lady: source key thyroid nuclear scan, but the compilers thought CT neck — see explanation. 426

Biopsy

  • Incisional → remove part of the lesion. Excisional → remove the entire lesion. Core needle → tissue core preserving architecture. FNA → cells for cytology.
FNACore biopsyIncisionalExcisional
What is obtained?CellsCore of tissuePart of lesionEntire lesion
Cytology✓✓✓✓
Tissue architectureLimitedYesYesYes
InvasivenessLowestLowHigherHigher
Typical exampleThyroid noduleBreast massLarge lesion when core is unsuitableLymph node
Definitive treatment?NoNoNoSometimes
  • Also: punch (superficial lesions) and endoscopic biopsy (mucosa/submucosa).
  • Myth: biopsy routinely spreading cancer is incorrect.
  • Parathyroid cancer: the sample is taken as frozen section at surgery (FNA is avoided — risk of seeding). 435

Histopathology & IHC

  • Confirm malignancy (benign vs malignant); histological type (adenocarcinoma, SCC, lymphoma, sarcoma); differentiation/grade; subtype (e.g. mucinous adenocarcinoma); IHC profile (lineage, likely primary).
  • IHC: antibodies detect specific proteins. Purposes: tumor type → cytokeratin (carcinoma), CD45 (lymphoma); primary origin → CDX2/SATB2 (colorectal), PAX8 (renal/Müllerian); guide treatment → ER/PR/HER2; proliferation → Ki-67; molecular pathway → MMR proteins (MLH1, PMS2, MSH2, MSH6); sarcoma → CD117/DOG1 (GIST).
IHC markerAssociation / use
CK7Breast, lung, ovarian, pancreatobiliary, urothelial
CK20Colorectal and urothelial
CDX2Intestinal/colorectal
SATB2Colorectal/appendiceal
TTF-1Lung adenocarcinoma and thyroid
PAX8Renal, thyroid, Müllerian
ER/PRBreast & gynecologic; predict hormonal therapy
HER2Breast, selected gastric/GEJ; predict targeted therapy
PSA/NKX3.1Prostatic origin
Synaptophysin, Chromogranin ANeuroendocrine
S100/SOX10Melanocytic and neural
Melan-A/HMB45Melanoma
CD117 (KIT)GIST
DesminSmooth muscle (leiomyosarcoma)
  • Cancer of unknown primary: metastasis found but primary not seen → biopsy the metastasis (liver/peritoneum) → IHC panel to estimate origin; molecular profiling guides therapy.
  • Submucosal gastric mass with normal mucosa and central ulceration, presenting with hematemesis → GIST (CD117). 436
  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis + rapidly enlarging diffuse goitre → thyroid lymphoma. 435
  • Malignant tumor of the parafollicular C cells = medullary carcinoma (calcitonin). 427
  • Diagnostic pre-treatment tumor marker in thyroid cancer (keyed) → calcitonin (medullary); thyroglobulin is for follow-up after total thyroidectomy in differentiated cancer. 437 Final ×2
  • Malignant lung tumor among the options: carcinoid. 427

8. Staging

  • Complete staging work-up (cancer-specific): local staging + distant metastasis.
  • Clinical staging: TNM for most solid tumors; FIGO for ovarian/cervical/endometrial; WHO for brain tumors.
  • Purposes: define extent, assess prognosis, plan treatment. → MDT discussion.
  • Common staging imaging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (CT CAP); gastric cancer may need diagnostic laparoscopy ± PET.
  • Colon (splenic-flexure) adenocarcinoma → staging by CT chest, abdomen and pelvis. 429 Final
  • Biopsy-proven gastric adenocarcinoma → next step CT scan (staging) — EUS and diagnostic laparoscopy come after. 433 Final
  • Staging colon cancer = CT chest, abdomen & pelvis. 427
StageRectal cancer — extent of invasion (doctor)
T1Submucosa
T2Muscularis propria
T3Beyond muscularis propria into mesorectal/perirectal tissue (depth matters)
T4aPenetrates the visceral peritoneal surface
T4bDirectly invades adjacent organs
  • T4 disease has a high recurrence risk even with negative nodes.

Staging tools: CT (liver metastasis), diagnostic laparoscopy, PET-CT

  • Breast cancer prognosis depends mainly on the number of positive axillary lymph nodes. 427 429 Final ×2
  • Sentinel node biopsy in breast cancer = to assess the extent of lymphatic (axillary) involvement. 441

  • Clinical pearl: male with a retroperitoneal mass → examine the testes.

9. MDT: resectability & operability

  • Resectability: can the tumor technically and oncologically be completely removed?
  • Operability: fitness for surgery — can the patient safely tolerate the operation?
  • Cancer factors + patient factors + treatment options → MDT decision.
  • A tumor may be resectable but the patient inoperable. Unresectable tumors may be converted to resectable by treatment, or palliated.
  • MDT may choose surgery first, chemotherapy first, radiation first, combined, or palliative care.

10. Surgical management

Curative surgery

  • Complete removal of the cancer with adequate margins and appropriate regional lymph-node management, preserving function when possible: oncological resection, en-bloc resection.
  • Resection margins: R0 = no microscopic residual; R1 = microscopic residual; R2 = macroscopic residual.
  • Cytoreductive surgery.
  • En bloc: tumor + directly involved adjacent organ(s) removed together without cutting through the tumor plane (e.g. colon cancer invading bladder/uterus → resect with the colon).
  • Margins depend on pathology: lipoma needs no wide margin; sarcoma/dermatofibrosarcoma ~2–4 cm; inadequate margin → re-excision.

Palliative surgery

  • Surgery without expectation of cure — to relieve symptoms or prevent major complications:
    • Obstructing unresectable colorectal cancer → diverting colostomy or bypass.
    • Unresectable gastric cancer causing obstruction → gastrojejunostomy.
    • Other indications: bleeding, obstruction, perforation, pain, infection.
  • Goal = symptom control and quality of life — important even in metastatic disease: palliative resection, stent, diverting stoma, feeding tube, pain procedures, bypass.
  • Why operate on incurable cancer? To improve quality of life. 439 ×2
  • Obstructing rectosigmoid/low rectal cancer with liver and lung metastases → diverting stoma (transverse colostomy). 435 ×2 437
  • 89-year-old, obstructing sigmoid cancer with liver + lung metastases: source key colectomy (palliative resection) — see the explanation for the debate. 439

11. Multimodal treatment

  • Surgery; systemic therapy (chemotherapy, targeted, immunotherapy, hormonal); radiotherapy (external beam, local techniques).
  • Neoadjuvant: before definitive surgery. Adjuvant: after surgery. Perioperative: before and/or after. Definitive: primary curative modality. Palliative: symptom control/prolonging life.
  • Local/regional therapies: RFA, microwave ablation, cryoablation, TACE.
  • Maintenance therapy = lower-intensity prolonged therapy to delay progression.
  • Melanoma: immunotherapy can produce major/complete responses.
  • Rectal cancer — TNT (total neoadjuvant therapy): chemo + radiotherapy before surgery → ~30–40% complete clinical response, allowing selected patients to avoid immediate resection under close surveillance.
  • Chemotherapy after resection = adjuvant. 435
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy role = local and metastatic (systemic) control. 439
  • Locally advanced low rectal cancer (T3N1M0), not obstructed → start with (chemo)radiation (neoadjuvant), not upfront surgery. 437
  • Neoadjuvant radiotherapy role in rectal cancer → down-stage the tumor 436; neoadjuvant radiotherapy = local control. 435 ×2
  • Wait ~3 weeks after oncologic resection before chemotherapy (proliferative phase of wound healing). 435 · 438 Final ×6
  • HCC on cirrhosis within Milan criteria (single ≤5 cm, Child B) → liver transplant. 438 ×3 438

12. Surveillance

  • Planned follow-up after treatment to detect recurrence or new cancers: history & exam, tumor markers, imaging, endoscopy, organ-specific tests; further investigation if recurrence suspected.
  • Colorectal: ~95% of recurrences within 2 years, nearly all by ~3 years; intensive surveillance largely finished by 5 years.
  • Slow-growing tumors (some sarcomas) may recur late → surveillance up to ~10 years.
  • "When is she cured?" → a normal duration of life without further clinical or radiological evidence of cancer. 439

13. Summary — strategy for cancer treatment

  • Possible neoadjuvant therapy to render the primary operable.
  • Radical surgery for the primary.
  • Lymph nodes: radical excision (e.g. gastric cancer) or sampling (e.g. breast cancer).
  • Adjuvant therapy based on pathologic staging (e.g. chemo for node metastases).
  • Radical surgery for distant metastases (e.g. excision of liver or lung metastases).
  • Palliative surgery for symptom relief if cure is not possible.

Other organ facts asked under oncology

  • Esophageal cancer predispositions: achalasia, Plummer-Vinson, Barrett's, corrosives — esophageal cyst is NOT precancerous. 427 426
  • Esophageal cancer: most common symptom is progressive dysphagia. 426
  • Barrett's esophagus predisposes to adenocarcinoma; it is not resected in the metaplasia phase (surveillance). 426
  • Benign esophageal tumors: leiomyoma, fibrovascular polyp, papilloma — leiomyosarcoma is malignant. 426
  • Palliation in esophageal cancer: stents, radiotherapy/brachytherapy, chemo (incomplete old question). 426
  • Paget's disease of the nipple = superficial manifestation of an underlying breast cancer. 426
  • Fibroadenoma: usually < 5 cm and well encapsulated ("large >5 cm, not capsulated" are wrong). 426
  • Cholangiocarcinoma is most common at the bifurcation of the hepatic ducts (Klatskin). 426
  • Liver lesions: metastases are the commonest malignant liver lesion (incomplete question). 426
  • Parotid malignant feature: skin ulceration (also facial nerve palsy, fixity). 426
  • Marjolin ulcer → SCC arising in a chronic scar/burn. 426
  • Commonest melanoma type: superficial spreading. 427
  • Picture of an ulcerated skin lesion → SCC. 435
